[interposing] You’re welcome. CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: you know, hopefully that is a really amazing testimony for other folks

that are watching, other veterans that deserve that same level of treatment and resource, that they hear that experience and are able to see that as their push to self-identify and come get some services. I will yield for my questions as I have— I don't have any more, but thank you so much for answering our questions today.
You're welcome.

And, Executive Director Smalls, thanks not only for your service to the country but being so willing to share your personal story with the committee. I know, it's gotta be a very emotional and very challenging thing to share in such a public forum, but I think it really illustrates exactly what we're trying to get across here today.

Thank you. Um, you know, I, I tell the veterans that I come into contact with, sharing my story gives other people the opportunity to share their story. And sometimes, you know, veterans like myself, we're scared because we don't know who we can trust. Because we have endured so many traumas, either due, you know, our personal

lives or serving, and just being able— being the person that someone could feel comfortable with, I I can share my story anytime. So yes, thank you for hearing it.

Thank you. Uh, Commissioner, the– you know, it's, it's no secret that in spite of— and I know you're new, so, uh, maybe you can't answer this question as fully as you might be six months from now, but I'll go ahead and ask it anyway. Uh, you talked about the Department of Veterans Affairs and their data sharing and the different things that they're doing. The— it's no secret that in spite of the warm personal relationship that the president enjoys with the mayor, that there are a lot of fundamental differences that the national administration has with city government and state government in New York that manifests itself in transportation issues, immigration issues, finance issues. From what you can tell, what level of cooperation overall are you experiencing from the federal Department of Veterans Affairs and any other relevant federal agencies?

So at DVS, and I think that is a very important question because we're

trying to make that distinction of what DVS is, right? So, at DVS, We are just a sole connector. We are a city agency, a New York City agency. So that is the— sometimes the confusion that people do have, whether, they think of us as the Veteran Affairs and they think that anything that happens at a federal level, that we are also connected or that we have, I would like to say some sort of pull to be able to change whatever happens at a federal level. So I think what we're trying to make clear is that at DVS, we are just so the sole connector in that whatever happens at a federal level, we try our best to communicate it, whether that is through the city agencies or the, or the city partners that we have. And so I think to that response, I would just stick to that we are just the sole connector at a city agency and not responsible for what happens at a federal level.
But then you wouldn't characterize them from what you could tell as being uncooperative thus far?

So to my understanding, but what we are seeing is that when there is something that does happen at a federal

level, advocates themselves in New York City— when I say advocates, veteran advocates— will make it very clear what is the— what are certain changes that do need to happen. And I think maybe an example can be the, um, disability— how the disability was being– the disability concern that, that just came up from a federal of when you could–
[interposing] You can just— is that the Richard Starr Act? No?

So this was separate. This came up a couple of weeks ago where there was some conversations around disability benefits being pulled back once medication treated some sort of illness. And this was something where the advocates, whether that be from VFW, American Legion, or individual veteran advocates, have spoke up about what issues that can cause, how detrimental to the community that can be. And that was actually something that was automatically rescinded. So for us, it's recognizing that we're hearing the community on the ground level and being able to make sure that they have the voice to speak their truth and what they need to happen.

And, and I think just adding to that, that was the sole responsibility of DVS of what was happening at a federal level. We were just letting them know, connecting them to that information. But again, I think veteran advocates will add— will make it very clear of what are their needs. And I think that is a very— that's why it's very important that many of them are here today to emphasize what is working, what is not working, and what needs to happen at a city level.

All right, my last question is in your testimony, Commissioner, you alluded to a lot of female veterans not self-identifying because of stigma and past experience. What can city agencies do to create a safer and more welcoming environment for female veterans to encourage that degree of self-identification?

One, one of the things that— I'm going to give an example. One of the things that DVS has done is partner up with, um, the Mayor's Office of People with Disabilities to provide them with military cultural competency of what, what is– because it's one thing when you are— when it

comes to disabilities, right, dealing with someone who is from a veteran that experienced other sort of, of physical harm when, when in the military, or during their service per se. It— you need another type of level of military culture competency. I think it even comes when it comes to like, it— when dealing with— there's many nonprofits, an example out there, that provide amazing services, but because they are not “veteran designated.” There's many missed opportunities for veterans to go and get the support that they need there. But oftentimes too, if they do go, there's not that cultural competency, right? So I think at DVS, um, as the military family advocate program that we do, that we launched out of Staten Island, right? That is something that we're trying to bring in all 5 boroughs. But additionally, as DVS, we want to connect with— first, I want to talk to the veteran groups first to know, like, how can we provide services to city agencies and other partners, uh, when it comes to military culture competency. I also want to have their say on this, but that is something that as an agency we're going to start working on.

Thank you, Commissioner, not only for your testimony here today and for your service to the people of the city of New York, but for you and your family's service to the country in the military. Appreciate it very much.

Thank you all, and thank you for giving us this opportunity. Again, as I know my testimony also ran longer, but I think this was an opportunity that oftentimes women don't get the opportunity to speak out on what's going on. And thank you for giving me that chance to talk about what women veterans go through. And I'm really looking forward to also hearing all the testimonies from all the advocates too, to know what as an agency we need to work on and how I can better support them, too.

Thanks very much. Thank you, Executive Director Smalls and Ms. Orlando as well. All right, we are going to open the hearing for public testimony at this point. I'll remind members of the public that this is a formal government proceeding and that decorum shall be observed at all times. As such, members of the public shall remain silent at all times. The witness table

is reserved for people who wish to testify. No video recording or photography is allowed from the witness table. Further, members of the public may not present audio or video recordings as testimony, but may submit transcripts of such recordings to the Sergeant-at-Arms for inclusion in the hearing record. If you wish to speak at today's hearing, please fill out an appearance card with the sergeant-at-arms and wait to be recognized. When recognized, you'll have two minutes. Might— if we're feeling generous, might give you an extra minute to speak on today's hearing topic, which is serving women veterans. We will hear all in-person testimony first and then turn testimony on– turn to testimony on Zoom. If you have a written statement or additional written testimony you wish to submit for the record, please provide a copy of that testimony to the Sergeant-at-Arms. And by the way, thank you to the Sergeants-at-Arms for the great work they've done today, as always. I'll now call the first panel: Ashton Stewart, Derek Coy, Ronald Reid. Please come on up and be heard.

Good morning. My name is Ashton Stewart. Thank you, Chair Morano and thank you, Chair Farías and members of the New York City

Council Committee on Veterans and Women Gender Equity for holding this hearing. You'll see before you, I've got a long four-page testimony. I'm just going to highlight some of the things here. There is an attachment that I will bring up as well. I am the Veterans Program Manager for MJHS Hospice Palliative Care and the MJHS Health System. We're the not-for-profit organization and the second largest hospital provider in the region. I'm also a Navy veteran and a veteran who served in the First Gulf War during Desert Shield. We have served hundreds of veterans in our programs. Really, we've stepped it up because I got my certification as a Veteran Service Officer in 2024. We've served many women veterans, including a 107-year-old from your council district, Paladino, who served in the Women's Air Corps, whose family informed us that she she was denied VA healthcare, and we reminded them that despite her income, that in 2023, they announced that all World War II veterans are eligible for no-cost healthcare at the VA. After admission to the MJHS Hospice, we are able to secure additional support from the VA for her, helping to take off some much-needed respite for the caregivers, and we recognize her service. That

set the stage for future generations of female service members. We presented her with the Veterans Day proclamation signed by New York State Governor Hochul. We helped get the medals that she would never received, that she had earned 80 years ago. And it was just such an honor to meet her and support her. We also had another veteran who was one of the first to get the COVID shot at the Manhattan VA. She was a pediatrician in the Army and retired, and we helped the family arrange for her to be reunited with her husband after giving her also a veteran recognition ceremony in the VA cemetery in Puerto Rico. This pocket card is to address clinicians. We developed this with the State Department of Veterans Services because of the gap that was identified by a RAND study in 2018 that only two percent of public and private providers are even asking a question if somebody served. We pared it down to seven simple questions leading with our– did you serve in the US military? And then the sensitive approach, “Is it okay if I talk with you about your military experience?” These QR codes are essential. Restoration of Honor is for women who are victims of MST. The transgender population who is getting booted

out of the service right now, the Restoration of Honor will help them get upgraded to honorable if they find themselves with another than honorable discharge. It's wonderful legislation that is, of course, advertised here as well. So early detection is key and essential to supporting veterans. Thank you so much for the opportunity to share this with you today.
Thank you.
Thank you. My name is Ronald Reid. I'm the—
[interposing] Nice and close, Mr. Reid, to the mic, if you would.

Thank you. My name is Ronald Reid. I am a veteran, Army veteran. I am the SAGE Vets Program Manager, a New York State program that supports LGBTQ+ adults over 50 at SAGE. SAGE is the nation's oldest and largest organization dedicated to LGBTQ+ older adults. Since 1978, we've worked to ensure that LGBTQ+ elders, veterans, and older New Yorkers living with HIV can age with dignity and support. We provided services and advocacy that combat isolation, promote health, wellness, expand access to affirming housing and care, advance

policies that protect LGBTQ+ elders. I would like to share a story that speaks to these issues. We recently worked with a 78-year-old white bisexual veteran living in Manhattan. He served honorably in the U.S. Army during the Vietnam era, a time when he was being open about his identity would have cost him everything. Decades later, he still lives with this impact that– of that service, chronic back, neck, and foot pain from intense physical training, along with mental health disabilities that affects his daily life, trying to find housing that is affordable with an elevator or not a fourth-floor walk-up. Providing veterans with a mission preference for public housing is a direct way to honor their service and provide them with stability and support needed to thrive in civilian life. This is especially important for LGBTQ+ veterans experiencing housing instability who may have been denied access to benefits available to others. Thank you.
Thank you for your testimony, and thank you for your service as well.

Hello, Derek Coy. Thank you, Chairperson Farías and Morano and members of the committee for the opportunity to testify on behalf of

the New York Health Foundation. My name is Derek Coy, and I'm a senior program officer at NY Health. I'm also a former sergeant in the United States Marine Corps and veteran of the Iraq War. For nearly 20 years, NY Health has supported numerous organizations, including city agencies, to understand and address the health needs of New York's veteran population, with a particular focus on women veterans. Women have served this nation honorably in every war since our founding— our nation's founding, often in unacknowledged roles, yet full gender equality in military service remained out of reach for generations. Since the cap on female participation was lifted in 1973, the number of women serving has grown steadily. Today, women are the fastest-growing segment of the veteran population and are younger and more racially diverse when compared to their male counterparts. Despite this growth, significant gaps remain in our understanding of women veterans' health and well-being, particularly on highly consequential issues such as suicide and justice involvement. At NY Health, we've invested in research to help close these gaps, such as the first comprehensive review of veterans' health and social

service needs in 14 years, as well as a study of minority veterans in New York State, both of which centered women's voices in the process. We offer several findings as a resource to inform the committee's work in our written testimony, but since my time here is limited, I would like to harp on a few that I believe are paramount. Research indicates that women veterans face distinct barriers to accessing care and other support. A 2020 Syracuse University study of women in the military found that more than half did not feel prepared to navigate resources in their community after their time in service, compared to just 37 percent of their male counterparts. This likely contributes to one of the most pressing issues veterans face, that of suicide. Tragically, veteran suicide remains a chronic problem, and mortality data underscores this disproportionate risk women veterans face. In 2022, the national suicide rate for women veterans was 92 percent higher than for non-veteran women. We know veterans involved in the justice system are twice as likely to die by suicide compared to veterans with no history of criminal justice involvement. At the same time, women have become the fastest-growing

incarcerated population in the U.S. However, there is limited data on women veterans' involvement with the justice system. Beyond these sobering facts, it is hard to fully grasp the complex and intersecting dynamics of suicide, justice involvement, and gender since they are often underrepresented in data and surveys due to privacy concerns and small population sizes. Without timely, reliable, disaggregated data, women veterans remain statistically invisible even as disparities persist. To better serve women veterans, we urge the City Council to consider closing these critical data gaps, equipping the broader health system and community providers to better meet the unique needs of women veterans, and strengthening outreach and engagement to women veterans specifically. We appreciate and share the council's focus on women veterans. With better data, stronger coordination, and targeted outreach, New York City can lead in ensuring that women veterans are not only recognized, but fully supported. I hope that you will look to myself and the foundation as a partner and resource for this work, and thank you for your time on this critically important topic.

Thank you for your testimony, Mr. Coy, and for your service. And I know you didn't get to the entirety of your testimony, especially about the very important aspects of strengthening outreach and engagement. We will all read that thoroughly, and that will absolutely be a part of the committee's record. Thank you for putting in so much work, and all three of you for such well-prepared testimony today. Appreciate it.
Thank you.

Thank you. All right, at that point, we'll call our next panel: Michael Matos, Coco Culhane, and Dr. Remolia Simpson. Apologies if I mispronounce anyone's name. Please correct me when you get a chance. Go ahead when you're ready.

Good afternoon, Chair Murano, Chair Farías, committee members. My name is Michael Matos, and I serve as the President of Five Borough Veterans. Our sole purpose is to strengthen the position of New York City's military-connected community through advocacy, civic engagement and legislative action, ensuring that we are not just heard by decision makers in this city, but that we

help shape its future. I grew up in NYCHA housing. That's not a detail I mentioned for sympathy, but because I know what public housing actually means to a family that has nothing else. It served as the difference between a stable foundation and critical instability, and is a resource that too many veterans in this city struggle to access right now. I served in the United States Coast Guard. When I left, I had the benefit of having people around me who helped me stabilize. Not every veteran does. NYCHA houses one in 17 New Yorkers and has the legal authority under both state law and federal regulation to give veterans a preference in admissions. It has simply chosen not to. There is an unchecked box in NYCHA's admissions preference form. Domestic violence survivors have this preference, as well as intimidated witnesses. We're asking that those who serve this country be extended the same consideration. Next week, on March 10th, Five Borough Veterans will be on the ground for the city's annual Hope Count, going street by street to find our homeless veterans, make sure they're counted, and connect them to resources. Veterans living on the street are often more willing to talk to someone who

shares their bond of service, so we'll be there. What we need is something to offer them. NYCHA should be one of those options. This hearing also takes up the question of how this city serves women veterans, and that matter deserves equal attention. Five Borough Veterans looks forward to hearing from our women veteran advocates on what they need so we can focus on taking the legislative action required to support them effectively. On both fronts, the path forward is the same: identify the gap and close it. NYCHA has been asked four times since 2004 to include a veteran's preference in their agency plan. We are here to make sure it happens, and we intend to stay at the table until it is done. The process exists. The authority exists. What's needed now is the will. Thank you.

Thank you, Mr. Matos. One quick question, for me, and I'm looking forward very much to working with you over the next couple of years to help a lot of veterans. In the most recent count that you've done of unsheltered homeless veterans. Can you estimate approximately what the unsheltered homeless veteran population is in New York City?

So that's the concern, Chair Morano. So we spoke with the NYC Department of Social Services on the last count. Now we're a brand new agency, so we haven't done an account ourselves, but the reason why we're doing this, the Hope Count next week is because we specifically asked DSS what metric they use to measure how many veterans are out in the street, and there is none. So the reason why we're going out there is we created our own metric, and we're gonna go find them ourselves, hand them over to DVS for proper connection, and ensure that working for– moving forward with DSS, they establish their own metrics so we don't have to go do it ourselves.
I hope you'll keep the committee posted.
Absolutely.
Thank you very much.
Of course.
Please.

Hi. I'm Coco Culhane, the Executive Director of Veteran Advocacy Project. We provide free legal services to veterans and their families, and we focus on working with those

individuals who have post-traumatic stress, brain injury, substance use issues, other mental health conditions. So we really work with a small subpopulation of veterans who are extremely vulnerable. And so instead of going through— I have a lot of stats and policy sort of stuff in my testimony. I just wanted to make a few points and share a client's story. You know, I think the need for accurate data, as you were just talking about with homeless vets, you know, I mean, every year at the hearing DHS talks about how they know their names and they know where all six of them are, and it drives me mad because we have at least that many people in our database already. So I think the need for accurate data is really important. But more than that, the voices of women veterans need to be heard. What are the practical realities behind those numbers? What are they actually experiencing? I'm a civilian. I don't pretend to speak for anyone, but I think that is really important. So often, you know, how these laws and these different policies play out are not exactly what's intended. So getting the facts on the ground for people who are impacted by them, I think is so important. And the other thing I wanted

to touch on is the impact of systemic racism. It's what we see in addition to focusing on mental health. That is probably the largest trauma that we see among our clients. And if you look at statistics about service members, it impacts discipline and discharge rates, and a person's discharge status determines what access to benefits and healthcare that they have. So, just to give you a quick statistic. Something like, I think 60 percent of women veterans are white, 53 percent of our clients are women who are Black, 83 percent are women of color. So you see there an incredible imbalance. And so I just– if I may share—
[interposing] Please.

the story, a client story. I think it exemplifies some of the challenges. And again, this is among the most vulnerable individuals, but we had a woman who served in the Navy's— in the Navy in the early 1980s. She was doing quite well, and she was then raped in her barracks. She turned to alcohol and then marijuana. She was discharged other than honorably, and she spent the next 35 years being unsheltered, struggling with addiction, and she had a stroke, she had lung cancer. She finally found

supportive housing and then was facing eviction because she was, you know, trying to get by on Supplemental Security Income. She had never told anyone she was a veteran ever in those decades. She was referred to VAP for services, and we represented her in housing court, in public benefits. But we also represented her with her VA claim and the Department of Defense to get a discharge upgrade. And what she experienced was that despite the fact that there were medical records showing she'd gotten pregnant, despite, you know, all of the different providers that she had gone to for her PTSD, the Board of Correction of Naval Records denied her upgrade because one record said that she was 29 when she was raped, and they pointed out she would have been out of the Navy for 2 years at that point. So one number that may have been a typo among thousands of pages are what has held her back. On the VA side, she was granted service connection for her PTSD. They believed her, but a procedural error has kept her case— kept her from getting the monetary benefits that go with that. And so we appealed it. She has been waiting more than three years just on that appeal. Her claim started six years ago. Last month I

received an email from the VA saying that she is 9,306th in line for a hearing. So that's some of the realities, you know, that people are struggling with, and not all women veterans, obviously, but those are the ones I think we have a responsibility to make sure that we're creating programs and reaching out to. So thank you for your time today.

Thank you, Ms. Culhane. And, you may say that you're not here to speak for anyone, but something tells me there are a whole lot of veterans that are glad you're speaking for them. And on March 10th, we're going to be doing a roundtable, myself, Councilmember Salaam, and Councilmember Banks on issues specifically facing Black veterans. It’s going to be right here, and I hope you'll come to that as well. Okay, Dr. Simpson?
Hi, my name is Dr. Simpson. Remolia Simpson is my name.
Thank you.

And I'm here on behalf— well, first of all, I'm a U.S. Army veteran. I've served six active duty years and 10 inactive duty years. Okay. We work as— when I say we, I mean just us volunteers because we hear what the problem is. So

we just do work as a volunteer, like veterans volunteer, and in the trenches, basically. So, and we proudly support DVS in this ongoing effort and safe support— I'm sorry, and secure, safe, and stable housing for the veterans and families in need. In the past year alone, we have proudly served— and Executive Director Donée Smalls doesn't even know this— we've proudly served 102 veterans, just us on the ground. So thank you, Commissioner. Thank you, DVS, again for that. Helped providing them connections to essential services, resources. We specialize in assisting veterans impacted by military sexual trauma. Drawing from lives– drawing from lived experience to provide compassionate, informed, and peer-centered support. Their leadership and partnership strengthened our ability to deliver meaningful volunteer services that directly assist local nonprofit organizations such as NAAM House, N-A-A-M House, and My Brother's House, through collaboration, shared resources, and coordinated– and coordination to housing solutions while reinforcing the community support system that empowers those who have served.

Thank you very much. Thank you. At this point, I'll invite our final in-person witness, Mr. Joe Bello of New York Metro Vets to come on up, and then we'll get to Zoom testimony. Thank you. When you're ready, Mr. Bello.
Okay, before I begin, real quick, I just want to make a note that I do support the resolutions that were today. So I'd like to see them both pass.
Thank you.

Anything around data and education are real important, so. Chair Morano, Chair Farías, and members of the Veterans and Women Gender Equity Committees, thank you for holding this long overdue hearing. All veterans are entitled to the benefits they have earned, yet men and women often experience military service differently and return to civilian life with distinct needs. I appreciate this hearing as the last City Council hearing focused specifically on women veterans was held 2008, and that's when DVS was still the Mayor's Office of Veterans Affairs. So, since then, the landscape has changed. Our veteran population has aged. The number of women veterans have steadily grown. However, the

city's capacity to identify, measure, and proactively respond to their needs has not kept pace. I would like to make three central points on this. Nearly 15,000 Women veterans call New York City home, representing more than 10 percent of our veterans population and one of the fastest segments. Yet our policies, our reporting, and outreach systems have not kept pace with their growth or their distinct needs. First, we cannot serve what we do not measure. The city does not consistently punish— publish gender and race desegregated data on how many veterans interact with housing, health, and economic support systems. We lack borough-level outreach metrics aligned with where women veterans live, and we do not see outcome measures demonstrating whether services improve stability or security. A recent audit also found data insecurities and missing legally required reports from DVS. Without these reliable, transparent data, oversight weakens and resources may not reach those who need them most. Second, women veterans face elevated risks. Women who serve are significantly more likely to experience military sexual trauma, which have long-term impacts on health, employment, and housing stability. While the City has reduced the

overall number of homeless veterans dramatically, we do not publish homeless data by gender. That means we cannot determine whether women veterans face distinct barriers or disparities in housing access. Third, outreach from DVS remains largely reactive. Delays in responding to VetConnect items can delay assistance such as housing requests, which can mean eviction or even having to go into shelter. I agree with the Commissioner that Local Law 37 has the potential to improve identification across city agencies. But it was passed in 2024, and implementation and public reporting are not complete. I also— there we go. I would also urge, besides the implementation of Local Law 37, quarterly disaggregated reporting, and having DVS consider publication of a women veterans strategic plan with measurable goals, outcomes, and timelines. Women veterans have served with distinction. They deserve city systems that see them, measure their needs accurately, and respond effectively. Thank you.

Thank you very much for your testimony. All right, thank you to all of you who came here to share your thoughts and experiences today. If there's anyone in the room who

wishes to speak but has not yet had the opportunity to do so, please raise your hand and fill out an appearance card with the Sergeant-at-Arms at the back of the room. But barring that, that concludes the in-person portion of our public testimony. So we'll now move to remote testimony. If you're testifying remotely, please listen for your name to be called. Once your name’s called, a member of our staff will unmute you. You may then start your testimony once the Sergeant-at-Arms sets the clock and cues you to begin. We will begin with someone who I'm not sure if I've ever heard testify at one of these hearings before, Christopher Leon Johnson.
You may begin.

Yeah, hello, my name is Christopher Leon Johnson. I support all the resolutions on this ticket, but I want to make this clear that I pray that this new Commissioner, Ysidia Mata, succeeds in her position as DVS Commissioner. But I want to make this clear that I think that next time when we have the pre-budget hearings, they should start questioning her about, like, what was that situation with her with ICE, her getting at the ICE agent to tell him, get the f-out.

CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: I'm going to stop you there, and if you do not remain on topic, we will mute your microphone. So if you'd like to remain on topic and give testimony towards serving women veterans in New York City, you can't continue.
I am. Man, this— you got to calm down, okay? CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: Please do not tell me to calm down. What I need you to do is continue your testimony.
Okay, okay.
On topic.

Going forward, when it comes to women's veterans, if she's a woman veteran– I just want— when it comes to women's veterans, yeah when it comes— they need to prioritize women's veterans from getting NYCHA units over the people that– we could tell like they just sleep around all day and they just get— they get everything. It's just like, it shouldn’t be like that. People that serve this country first should get prioritized, that then the legal immigrants and people that just come fresh out of prison, like, who just completely like a criminal. That should be the

thing. Going with this resolution. Decline. Yeah, so– yeah, hello? Yeah, so basically in a nutshell, I support resolutions on the bill. Going forward, the veterans should be prioritized more than everybody else that like who just no good in the city. [inaudible] city where we prioritize the migrants and people that like commit all these crimes in the city, and they get put on a pedestal. They get parades and stuff like that, more than veterans.
Thank you, your time expired.
Thank you, Mr. Johnson.
Thank you.

All right, if there's anyone else currently on Zoom who wishes to speak, but has not yet had the opportunity to do so, please use the raise hand function and our staff will unmute you. If there's anyone else present in the room who's not had the opportunity to testify but wishes to do so, please raise your hand. And what I'll just add as a point of personal privilege for everybody. Obviously this is a group of people in the room that's very well connected in the veterans

community. This is one of the most important topics, women– serving women veterans in New York City that I could possibly think of for the City Council to address. And I'm grateful to the seven folks that testified in-person and even the one gentleman that testified via Zoom. But I can't help but think that there are dozens, maybe hundreds of other folks that we could have heard from today and either didn't know about the opportunity to testify at this hearing, or they weren't able to make themselves available to testify. To the extent that you're able– we're gonna be covering a lot of important subjects with this committee, and I know Chair Farías covers a lot of important subjects with her committee. I'd really appreciate it if you could spread the word throughout your circles, your social groups, your professional circles, your volunteer circles, that we're really eager for the testimony of veterans, particularly female veterans, and we're taking their feedback into into account as we formulate the next oversight steps and as we formulate legislation. I think there's a lot of folks that have a lot to add that we didn't necessarily hear from today. With that, I will invite Chair Farías to give her closing remarks.

CHAIRPERSON FARÍAS: You've said it all. This hearing is now adjourned. Gavel us out.

[gavel] Thank you, everyone.

The importance of trees to New Yorkers is obvious. They are the frontline in providing for a healthy environment. Trees improve water quality by filtering and diverting stormwater runoff, filter high frequency noises, and provide habitats for wildlife. They also help reduce the urban heat island effect, bring people closer to nature, cool the air

in hot weather, and improve air quality by reducing pollution. Various studies have estimated that trees reduce annual residential energy costs by 17 million dollars per year and reduce runoff by 69 million cubic feet per year. calls involve complaints about trees, including concerns over premature deaths to new trees, broken tree limbs and sidewalk damage resulting from growing tree roots. necessary to make equitable tree coverage and green space access a reality for all New Yorkers, no matter where you live or where you come from. All levels of government need to get serious in treating our tree stock as crucial infrastructure that must be supported with sufficient resources and equitably distributed to all parts of our city. We deserve no less, and the well-being of our environment and the health of each and every New Yorker depends on this reality.

I'd like to provide a quick update on the tree impact resulting from late February's Winter Storm Hernando, which produced the most significant impacts we've witnessed from a snowstorm since 2018. I'm grateful to our expert forestry crews at parks and to our partners on the Down Tree Task Force, including NYC Emergency Management, Department of Sanitation, FDNY, and NYPD, who worked as one team to respond to the reports we were hearing from the public and bring some normalcy back to our city. During the course of the storm, we received more than 1,800 tree-related service requests, which included a

significant portion of duplicate requests related to the same concern, as often happens during storms. After performing over 1,200 inspections, all of which were completed within 48 hours of the end of the storm, our foresters confirmed that a total of 220 fallen trees due to the storm, including 47 that were blocking streets and nine trees or large limbs that fell on buildings, all of which were addressed within 72 hours after the storm ended. We created over 1,000 work orders related to damaged or fallen trees and limbs and are completing that work as quickly as possible, prioritizing the most severe and dangerous conditions. To be clear, this can be complex and challenging work, especially in slippery and snowy conditions, involving the use of heavy equipment and large vehicles, so we thank New Yorkers for their patience and support as the work continues. Even outside of emergency extreme weather conditions, our agency is dedicated to caring for our trees in a way that keeps New Yorkers safe, so we utilize a rigorous risk management approach to prioritize tree conditions that present the most risk to the public and address those immediately. Our Forestry Team has taken steps in recent years to improve best practices in hopes of minimizing these negative impacts, such as enlarging our standard tree beds to allow more room for root growth, doing our best to avoid building damage due to tree limbs, and being more selective about the tree species being planted in a given location to avoid conflict with above-ground or below-ground infrastructure. Though it will take significant time before the full impact of these efforts are borne out, we are committed to continuing to seeking the best possible outcomes while protecting and nourishing this vital living infrastructure.

care and maintenance of our existing street trees and trees in landscape parks. And then to dial down into that, we also have approximately 250 active staff dedicated to caring for our trees, both in streets and in our landscape parks. That includes around 60 foresters and 90 climbers and pruners.

Thank you so much for your question. I love this question because it gives me an opportunity to publicly thank again the incredible work that our Park staff did, not just through this most recent storm, but in every storm. Parks is a 365-day operation. So, in extreme heat, we

are out there in our pools, beaches, in our parks, providing incredible services. Our recreation centers, our cooling centers, we do so much, but also in extreme cold, in extreme winter weather, we are also out there. Our Park staff dedicates our entire maintenance and operation team towards snow removal. And we have a very robust winter weather response plan that gets put out every year that prioritizes perimeter sidewalks, it prioritizes crosswalks, prioritizes high traffic areas in our parks, and then JOPs, jointly operated playgrounds, to make sure that those are also clear. After that, we go through a number of other spaces, but yes, we are deeply involved in snow removal. And we do, as part of that winter weather plan, as built into our operations, dedicate additional staff to our partner agencies at DSNY to help with that clearance. And we also dedicate some portion of vehicles to them. Our Mayor recently visited our Randall's Island Garage during the storm to see that Park staff are turning out and fixing our vehicles, fixing vehicles for other sister agencies, all throughout the night, throughout these storms, to make sure that we can deliver safe streets to all New Yorkers, and that includes sidewalks that

are a part of our responsibility because they're adjacent to parkland. Our foresters, in this most recent storm, our Forestry Unit, played an incredibly important role As I mentioned in my testimony, we had 1,800 service requests come in through 3-1-1 with New Yorkers reporting downed trees, downed limbs, that were blocking streets, that were on top of private property, that were needing to be addressed. And I am so proud of my team, including our Forestry Unit that's represented here today, for what they did to respond to that storm in a very quick and efficient way. We convened the Downed Trees Task Force, which is helped run by our partners at New York City Emergency Management, as part of the task force, FDNY, NYPD, Sanitation all serve on that task force where we are tracking in live time, real time, where we see downed trees, making sure that we're prioritizing getting those trees out of the streets so that emergency vehicles can get there. And then on top of that, then partaking trees and limbs off of properties, and then continuing to move down that list. From the most recent storm, we had over 1,000 work orders created. I want to again shout out my Forestry team and the Parks teams that came out and

cleared all of those streets within 72 hours of the storm's end, and we are just about getting finished with all of those work orders to date. Some of the last ones that we have on our list are really related to extra utilities work that needs to get done, or other kind of coordination that needs to get done. But overall, I'm incredibly proud of the role that Parks plays. Parks is a part of the sort of emergency response when it comes to these storms. And while we looked very much in partnership with NYCEM, with DSNY, with DOT, I'm very proud of the work that our staff does, and I know that many of them are listening in today. I know that many of them look very closely at hearings like this so, I want to give them their shout out and say thank you tremendously for the work that they did across the city because no part of the city was not affected by that storm.

I also want to say thank you to them as well. Just as a follow-up, particularly for the City Parks workers that were assigned to shovel and/or clear non-parks property, was their rate of pay consistent with that of the emergency snow shovelers who were hired per diem to clear public

areas such as the bus stops, crosswalks, and fire hydrants?

You know, I'll have to get back to you specifically on that. I can only speak for our staff so I don't know intimately the rate of pay for other workers at other agencies or how that works. We're happy to get back to you on that. But I will say that we understand that, I mean, snow shoveling is part of our responsibilities. When you look at our parkland, or specifically our landscaped parks, the sidewalk includes, that's our property, and we are responsible for clearing that. We understand that New Yorkers, many of them drive, but many of them walk. They take the buses. They bike to work. And so, we take that responsibility very seriously. And it's not something that I would ever look to kind of move to another agency exclusively because those are our sidewalks. We take a lot of pride in them. During the snowstorm, I myself went out to visit with teams. I myself helped clear a couple bus shelters and some crosswalks with those teams. It's a big job that I'm very proud that our team takes on, and I'm very proud of the partnership that we have with other agencies.

Given that partnership, and we definitely understand and appreciate Parks lending a hand to sister agencies, but in doing that, how is fairness assessed in the labor impact of assigning Park staff to assist in areas that really aren't Parks property?

Sure. I think that when it comes to our approach here, it really is looking at one city and looking at not through the boundaries of this is Park's job, this is DOT's job, this is DSNY's job, this is somebody else's job. Really and truly, we're looking at the lived experience of New Yorkers. We're making sure that when New Yorkers wake up after a snowstorm, when they're trying to get their kids to school, when they're trying to get to their jobs where they don't have the luxury of working from home or staying in on a snow day, that they can actually do that job. And so my goal as Commissioner of this agency is to make sure, yes, to fight for my team, yes, to highlight the work that they do, but ultimately to make sure that we can serve New Yorkers so that New Yorkers don't have to say, well, this is DOT's job, and this is New York Park's job when they step up here, and

this is another contractor's job, that ultimately New Yorkers just see clear sidewalks, that ultimately they are just able to get to their jobs, get to their kids, get to the groceries, and come home safely. So, I would just say that our team knows how much our job expands beyond the parks. We are always there to answer the call. We are always there to step up, and I'm so proud of the efforts that came in. Not only was our Park staff out early in the morning, 4 o'clock in the morning, overnight, our Park staff stayed in rec centers overnight to make sure that they could be there the next morning. It's about serving the city with comprehensive services.

And when it comes to quality assurance standards, do the forestry inspectors use when determining that a tree is in good or fair condition, I know that's normally the rating they get, especially when elected officials provide photos showing trees being damaged or protruding onto private property. Sure. Thank you, Council Member Banks, for that question. So, as the Commissioner mentioned, when we inspect trees, we take a tree risk management approach, which is what you're alluding to, and that's a very systematic methodology that's based on an industry standard that we've developed into a prioritization system to allow us to get to the most significant tree conditions first. So, that looks at the entire tree. Our inspectors look at the likelihood of a tree or any part of that tree failing or falling, the likelihood of that impacting people or property, and the consequences of that event, should it happen, right, how big is that tree, how big is that branch?
